translations.misc.virtual_location.title: Virtual location
translations.misc.virtual_location.scope: This page writes the coordinates as the Windows "system default location". It only affects programs that obtain their position through the Windows location service, and only when the system has no more accurate source. Browser web geolocation and apps with their own IP database or positioning SDK are unaffected. The change only touches the registry and can be undone at any time with "Clear virtual location".

translations.misc.virtual_location.action.force_provi: Also disable the Windows location provider so positioning falls back to the default location (system-wide)

Writes the policy DisableWindowsLocationProvider=1 to turn off the built-in Windows network positioning. Once disabled, apps that rely on real positioning (Maps, Weather, Find My Device) lose precise location; clear the checkbox to restore it.

This writes the policy DisableWindowsLocationProvider=1 and turns off the built-in Windows network positioning.

Once disabled, every app that relies on real positioning only gets the default location, and some system features (Weather, Maps, Find My Device) will lose precise positioning. Clear the checkbox to restore it.

translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.title: Blue Screen Buffer (Experimental)
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.warning: ⚠ The blue screen buffer modifies the ntoskrnl!KeBugCheckEx entry. It cannot repair the condition that caused the crash, cannot guarantee any usable time, and cannot prevent the system from ultimately failing. At trigger time Windows may already be corrupted, frozen, or unable to schedule your application; PatchGuard or security products may crash earlier. “Try to ignore the error” forcibly returns from a kernel path designed never to return and may immediately execute invalid code. Use only in isolated kernel-debugging environments.
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.persistence: This hook is off by default and one-shot: on a hit it restores the KeBugCheckEx entry before providing a buffer. Normal mode then enters conventional BugCheck; ignore mode only attempts to return to the caller and never means the system recovered. Disabling or unloading the driver restores an untriggered hook; never treat this as protection.
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.control.title: Experimental Controls
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.delay.tooltip: Only 1 to 30 seconds are allowed; the actual buffer may not work.
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.ack: I saved my work and understand this is not crash recovery and a forced return may immediately crash, deadlock, or corrupt data
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.try_ignore: After the buffer, try to ignore the current error and return to the caller (extremely dangerous)
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.try_ignore.to: KeBugCheckEx and its callers are designed never to return. A forced return may immediately execute invalid code, crash again, deadlock, or silently corrupt data; even if the system remains usable briefly, save immediately and force a restart.
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.screenshot: Immediately simulate Win+PrintScreen when the hook is hit
translations.misc.experimental.bugcheck.screenshot.to: R3 queries the hook state every 10 ms and sends Win+PrintScreen only once after a hit. The capture will fail if user mode, the input stack, DWM, or the current desktop can no longer be scheduled, and KSword cannot confirm that a file was saved.

translations.kernel.iotimer.detail.template:
IoTimer address: %1
DeviceObject: %2
DriverObject: %3
Driver: %4
Device: %5
Object path: %6
Image path: %7
Protocol version: %8
Field flags: 0x%9
Query status: %10

Safety boundary: the addresses come from the public WDK DEVICE_OBJECT.Timer field. For start/stop, R0 references the DriverObject again by name, validates the DeviceObject through a referenced device snapshot, and compares the PIO_TIMER. It only calls IoStartTimer/IoStopTimer and never dereferences or writes a private IO_TIMER.

Limitation: the WDM APIs return VOID, and Windows exposes no API to query the current enabled state of an IoTimer. Success means only that the public control API was called.
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.start.tooltip: Revalidate identity, then call IoStartTimer; the registered routine normally runs once per second
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.stop.tooltip: Revalidate identity, then call IoStopTimer; this may break the target driver's timeouts and state machine
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.start.risk: IoStartTimer enables the IoTimerRoutine registered by the target driver, normally once per second. Starting a driver that does not expect reactivation can cause reentrancy, device failure, or a system crash.
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.stop.risk: IoStopTimer stops the target driver's device-timer callback. It may implement timeouts, polling, recovery, or hardware keepalive; stopping it can hang the device, lose data, or crash the system.
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.warning_title: Critical risk: control an external driver's IoTimer
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.warning_text: You are about to perform “%1”. KSword reports the risk without restricting modification by Advanced Mode or risk level; target identity is still revalidated after you continue.
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.unsupported: The loaded KswordARK driver is too old and does not register the IoTimer control IOCTL. Update and reload the driver.
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.failed:
R0 refused the operation: %1
Semantic status: %2
NTSTATUS: 0x%3
Observed again: Driver=%4, Device=%5, Timer=%6

Refresh and confirm again if the identity changed or the target is invalid.
translations.kernel.iotimer.control.completed:
%1 was called after triple identity validation.

Windows IoStartTimer/IoStopTimer return VOID and expose no public runtime-state query. This result means the API accepted the call; it does not fabricate a verified running state.

translations.misc.render_benchmark.composition.hint: Lays a solid red panel and a solid blue panel on screen and moves an acrylic window between them, using BitBlt to capture the DWM-composed picture and average its color. That answers two things: whether the blur really takes effect (the sample should deviate from the panel's native color), and whether the blur still follows when nothing is done after the move. Colored panels appear on screen briefly during the run.
translations.misc.render_benchmark.drag.hint: Creates a test window shaped like the main window (frameless, transparent background, acrylic material, filled with a transparent table) and simulates a 60 fps drag, comparing the dropped-frame rate of repainting the whole tree on every material refresh against submitting the material only. A test window appears and moves by itself during the run, then closes automatically.
translations.misc.render_benchmark.repaint.hint: Renders the main window root container to an offscreen bitmap, measures one full repaint, and splits out what the background layer and the child widget tree each cost. With a transparent background every Dock surface is transparent, so a parent repaint redraws the whole widget tree; this test measures that cost. Measurement uses offscreen rendering and never touches the real interface on screen.
translations.misc.render_benchmark.response.hint: Simulates dragging the selected window with repeated SetWindowPos calls and round-trips a WM_NULL each frame to measure how long its UI thread stays blocked - a thread busy repainting cannot answer the empty message, so the round-trip time is the stall duration. Windows belonging to other processes can be measured too. The test only changes the window position and restores it afterwards; a maximized window cannot be moved, so restore it first.

context_translations.hardware.power.title: CPU Power and Performance Tuning
context_translations.hardware.power.scope: Windows power schemes use system APIs. Ring 0 tuning is limited to detected Intel RAPL/HWP/Turbo/requested-multiplier allowlisted fields. BIOS or microcode locks are never bypassed, and arbitrary MSR writes are not exposed.
context_translations.hardware.power.scheme.label: Current / target scheme
context_translations.hardware.power.risk_confirm: I understand that raising power or ratios can cause overheating, throttling, data errors, crashes, or reduced hardware life. I have saved my work and prepared a recovery path.
context_translations.hardware.power.boundary: Boundary: this page never tries to clear an MSR lock bit. Firmware, Windows power management, or another tuning tool may overwrite these values at any time. Model-specific AMD SMU/PBO writes are not implemented.
context_translations.hardware.power.confirm.title: Confirm CPU power change
context_translations.hardware.power.confirm.rapl: This will change package PL1/PL2 on every processor package. Excessive values may exceed cooling or power delivery; low values may severely throttle the CPU. Continue?
context_translations.hardware.power.confirm.turbo: This will change Intel Turbo Boost on every logical processor. Firmware or Windows may overwrite it. Continue?
context_translations.hardware.power.confirm.ratio: This will set every implemented MSR_TURBO_RATIO_LIMIT bin to the same ratio. A ratio beyond the CPU, motherboard, or cooling capability may immediately crash the system or corrupt calculations. Continue?
context_translations.hardware.power.confirm.requested_multipl: This will change the IA32_PERF_CTL requested multiplier on every logical processor. Speed Shift, firmware, or microcode may clamp or ignore the request; an excessive multiplier can cause overheating, crashes, or calculation errors. Continue?
context_translations.hardware.power.confirm.hwp: This will change HWP min/max/desired/EPP on every logical processor. These requests may compete with Windows power policy. Continue?
context_translations.hardware.power.confirm.raise: This will raise PL1/PL2 to the CPU-reported platform maximum of %1 W and disable clamp. It does not clear a BIOS/MSR lock and does not guarantee that the board, cooling, or firmware can sustain the value. Continue?
context_translations.hardware.power.confirm.restore: This will restore the Windows power scheme captured at the first valid refresh and all CPU fields that are still writable: PL1/PL2, Turbo, HWP, Turbo ratios, and the requested multiplier. Firmware or Windows may overwrite them again. Continue?

context_translations.driver.cleanup.title: sc Unload and Cleanup
context_translations.driver.cleanup.feature_name: sc unload and cleanup of the driver file and service registration
context_translations.driver.cleanup.confirm_body:
Target service: %1
Driver file: %2

This action is irreversible and will run strictly in this order:
1. Revalidate the current SCM configuration path and confirm that no other driver service shares the file.
2. Send SERVICE_CONTROL_STOP through SCM and wait for SERVICE_STOPPED.
3. Revalidate the configuration path and exclusive ownership after the stop.
4. Delete the service registration; delete the driver file only after that succeeds.

If stopping fails or SERVICE_STOPPED is not reached, neither the service registration nor the file will be deleted. If the service registration is deleted but file deletion fails, an orphaned file will remain and the service registration will not be recreated automatically; that partial-success state requires manual handling.

Continue?

context_translations.driver.confirm.destructive_unload.title: Force-teardown DriverObject
context_translations.driver.confirm.destructive_unload.body:
This operation bypasses the SCM/PnP lifecycle and always runs these stages in order:

1. Replace MajorFunction/FastIo with rejecting entry points
2. Force-terminate and wait for every system thread whose entry point is inside the driver image
3. Call DriverObject->DriverUnload when present
4. Detach upper/lower device relationships and delete every DeviceObject until DriverObject->DeviceObject is empty

If any thread cannot be confirmed stopped, DriverUnload is not called. This operation can immediately crash the system and is intended only for malicious-driver response.

Continue?

context_translations.driver.confirm.blind_irp.title: Blind IRP communication
context_translations.driver.confirm.blind_irp.body:
Target module: %1
DriverObject: %2
Object address: %3
Module base: %4

The following five communication entries will be replaced with the system rejection entry:
CREATE / READ / WRITE / DEVICE_CONTROL / INTERNAL_DEVICE_CONTROL

This does not unload the driver or stop its threads, callbacks, DPCs, shared-memory channels, or in-flight IRPs. Cleanup, Close, PnP, Power, SystemControl, Shutdown, and Fast I/O remain unchanged. The operation can still cause access failures, device faults, system hangs, or a bug check.

Entries that remain owned by this feature and were not changed by a third party can be undone with “Restore IRP communication”; conflicting entries are reported but never overwritten. Continue?

context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.execution_chain.t: The complete path from user mode to a driver
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.execution_chain.s: Put Win32 APIs, ntdll, system calls, kernel services, and driver dispatch in one execution chain instead of treating Ring 0 as unlimited authority.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.execution_chain.b:
### Object relationship

```text
Application -> Win32/NT API -> ntdll -> system call -> ntoskrnl/I-O manager -> driver
```

### Lifecycle
A calling thread starts a request and marshals parameters into the kernel. A synchronous request returns on that thread; an asynchronous one may finish in a completion routine, DPC, or worker. Process exit does not guarantee that kernel work is finished.

### Public and private boundary
Win32, selected NT APIs, and WDK dispatch contracts are documented. System-call numbers, internal service implementations, and private object layouts are not stable ABIs.

### Read-only observation path
Confirm caller identity and creation time in Processes, confirm the device and protocol in monitoring/driver status, then read the matching Kernel table together with its source.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Administrator identity is not kernel context. Driver callbacks are still constrained by thread context, requester mode, and current IRQL, and internal paths can change between builds.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: validate handles, lengths, status, and completion ownership at every layer. Incorrect: assume every pointer is trusted and every API callable after entering Ring 0.

### Ksword field interpretation
`source` identifies the observation layer, `status` is that layer's call result, and `unsupported/partial` says the chain is incomplete; they are not one verdict.

### What the evidence cannot prove
One successful IOCTL only proves that the current driver handled that request. It does not prove an unfiltered path, system-wide coverage, or that the target is safe.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.address_spaces.ti: Address coordinate systems and safe reads
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.address_spaces.su: Separate virtual and physical addresses, user and kernel addresses, RVAs, and file offsets so equal numbers are not mistaken for one location.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.address_spaces.bo:
### Object relationship

```text
File offset <-> PE section/RVA -> image virtual address -> page-table entry -> PFN/physical address
```

### Lifecycle
An RVA can be resolved only after an image mapping and load base exist. Virtual pages can disappear through faults, paging, protection changes, or process exit, and physical pages can be reassigned.

### Public and private boundary
PE sections and VirtualQuery results have public formats. Kernel page tables, the PFN database, and version-specific fields require supported APIs or validated DynData.

### Read-only observation path
Inspect virtual regions and protections in Memory, compare translation sources in Kernel SLAT/IOMMU, and verify image differences by section and RVA in the file scanner.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
A user address must be read in the correct process context; pageable addresses cannot be touched at excessive IRQL. LA57, large pages, VBS, and an IOMMU alter the translation layers.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: establish the coordinate system, range, process identity, and readability before a bounded copy. Incorrect: directly dereference an address supplied by a user or scan.

### Ksword field interpretation
Read `virtualAddress`, `physicalAddress`, `rva`, `fileOffset`, and `translationStatus` together. Zero has meaning only with the corresponding validity flag.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Translating one address does not prove that a whole span is contiguous or stable, belongs to the claimed module, or bypasses encryption and isolation.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.handles_reference: HANDLEs, object pointers, and reference ownership
Explain how handle values, object pointers, pseudo handles, kernel handles, and reference counts determine safe object lifetime.

### Object relationship

```text
Per-process handle value -> HANDLE_TABLE entry -> object header/body <- kernel pointer reference
```

### Lifecycle
Opening a handle increments the handle count and keeps a reference. Closing a handle and calling `ObDereferenceObject` release distinct ownership; destruction is possible only after the final reference disappears.

### Public and private boundary
HANDLE is opaque and routines such as `ObReferenceObjectByHandle` are documented. Handle-table encoding and object-header layout are version-specific internals.

### Read-only observation path
Read PID, handle value, type, and granted access in Handles, then correlate type, address, and reference status in Object Namespace or CID.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Validate user-supplied handles with `UserMode`; private driver handles should use `OBJ_KERNEL_HANDLE`. Reference and close operations must run in compatible context and IRQL.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: name who acquires a reference and who releases it on every exit path. Incorrect: copy a pseudo handle across processes or retain an object pointer without a reference.

### Ksword field interpretation
`handleValue` is process-local, `objectAddress` is transient kernel evidence, and `typeValidated` plus `referenceStatus` say whether decoding was safe.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A listed handle may no longer grant access and is not evidence of malice. Repeated object addresses across snapshots can also be allocator reuse.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.status_codes.titl: NTSTATUS, Win32 errors, HRESULT, and last error
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.status_codes.summ: Apply one set of rules to distinct error domains, success families, and the timing of GetLastError.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.status_codes.body:
### Object relationship

```text
Kernel NTSTATUS -> NT/Win32 conversion -> Win32 error -> optional HRESULT wrapper
```

### Lifecycle
A status can be converted at each return layer. Thread last-error state is read only after an API that promises to set it fails, and another call may overwrite it.

### Public and private boundary
`NT_SUCCESS`, Win32 errors, and HRESULT bit layouts are public. Custom driver status values must identify their source rather than masquerade as system codes.

### Read-only observation path
Start with Ksword's `status`, `win32Error`, `stage`, and raw hexadecimal value, then locate the layer that produced the error.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
The same error can represent privilege, length, capability, or a race. An IRQL violation often produces verifier failure or BugCheck instead of a useful status.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: identify the error domain before using its success predicate and formatter. Incorrect: treat every nonzero NTSTATUS as failure or read stale GetLastError after success.

### Ksword field interpretation
`stage` names the failing step, `lastStatus` carries NTSTATUS, `win32Error` is valid only on a Win32 path, and `message` is explanation rather than raw evidence.

### What the evidence cannot prove
`STATUS_ACCESS_DENIED` alone cannot distinguish missing rights, a protected process, policy filtering, or the wrong requester mode; the stage and input must be checked.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.irql_context.summ: Show how PASSIVE/APC/DISPATCH levels, the current thread, and waitability jointly constrain kernel APIs.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.irql_context.body:
### Object relationship

```text
Current CPU IRQL + current thread/process context -> accessible memory + callable APIs + waitability
```

### Lifecycle
IRQL rises and falls across interrupts, DPCs, dispatcher locks, and normal thread paths. The raiser must restore the old value on every path, and context switching requires a schedulable level.

### Public and private boundary
Each documented WDK API carries an IRQL contract. A private function that appears usable on one build cannot be assumed to have the same constraints.

### Read-only observation path
In Timer/DPC, Work-Queue Threads, and Callbacks, read source CPU, routine, execution class, and query status together rather than looking only at an address.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
`PASSIVE_LEVEL` permits waits and pageable code, `APC_LEVEL` is restricted, and `DISPATCH_LEVEL` or higher cannot block or touch pageable memory. Privilege never relaxes that contract.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: gather data at low IRQL and let high-IRQL paths consume only published nonpaged snapshots. Incorrect: perform file I/O, allocate paged pool, or wait in a DPC or crash callback.

### Ksword field interpretation
`executionClass`, `processor`, `routineAddress`, `module`, and `partial` describe context together. Do not invent an IRQL when the field is absent.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A routine inside a legitimate module can still violate its execution contract, and one snapshot cannot represent concurrent state on every CPU.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.synchronization.s: Separate spin locks, mutexes, ERESOURCEs, push locks, events, semaphores, atomics, and memory barriers by responsibility.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.synchronization.b:
### Object relationship

```text
Shared state -> atomics/barriers (visibility) + locks (exclusion) + events/semaphores (wait and wake)
```

### Lifecycle
Initialize a synchronization object, acquire and release it in a fixed order, then prevent new users and drain in-flight users before destruction. A wakeup does not guarantee that the condition remains true.

### Public and private boundary
WDK documents the IRQL, waitability, and recursion rules for each primitive. Internal lock fields, ranks, and undocumented objects must not be manipulated through offsets.

### Read-only observation path
Correlate producers and consumers in Timer/DPC, Work Queues, and Callbacks. Log times and thread IDs help reconstruct order but are not proof of locking.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Spin locks normally raise to DISPATCH_LEVEL; waitable locks require low IRQL. A memory barrier constrains ordering but does not provide ownership or sleep.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: define protected state, lock order, and cancellation paths first. Incorrect: wait while holding a spin lock, use volatile as synchronization, or skip predicate rechecks after an event.

### Ksword field interpretation
`sequence`, `threadId`, `processor`, `timestamp`, and `state` can expose races, but `snapshotTime` is only the sampling instant.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Failure to observe a collision does not prove race freedom, and stability on one CPU or under a debugger does not validate multiprocessor memory ordering.
Driver lifecycle from load to unload
Connect service configuration, the PE image, DriverEntry, DriverObject, DeviceObject, links, PnP, and unload cleanup.

### Object relationship

```text
Service configuration -> load PE -> DriverEntry -> DRIVER_OBJECT -> DEVICE_OBJECT/interface -> requests -> unload
```

### Lifecycle
A non-PnP driver usually creates a control device and unloads explicitly; a PnP driver's instances follow AddDevice and the device state machine. Unload must stop new requests, unregister callbacks, and drain work.

### Public and private boundary
DriverEntry, AddDevice, Unload, and WDF callbacks are public contracts. Loader lists and internal object fields are versioned read-only evidence.

### Read-only observation path
Correlate service, image, signature, and load state in Drivers; inspect Driver/Device objects and links in Object Namespace; then read the driver capability matrix.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Loading requires appropriate rights and signing policy. Unload normally runs at PASSIVE_LEVEL but must still coordinate DPCs, timers, WDF queues, and open handles.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: unwind resources in reverse registration order and give in-flight work explicit references. Incorrect: let callbacks touch an extension after deleting its device or assume stopping a service unloaded the image.

### Ksword field interpretation
`serviceState`, `imageBase`, `driverObject`, `deviceCount`, `signature`, and `unloadRoutine` come from different sources and may represent different instants.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A stopped service does not prove the driver is gone. A loaded image does not prove the device works, unload is safe, or its signature chain is currently trusted.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.wdm_kmdf.title: Responsibilities of WDM and KMDF
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.wdm_kmdf.summary: Explain how WDF requests and queues remain built on I/O-manager IRPs, objects, and completion rules.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.wdm_kmdf.body:
### Object relationship

```text
DeviceIoControl -> IRP/I-O stack -> WDFREQUEST/WDFQUEUE -> EvtIo* -> WdfRequestComplete
```

### Lifecycle
WDM manages IRPs and stacks directly. KMDF supplies request, queue, parent-object, and cleanup machinery, but underlying requests still follow I/O-manager and PnP/power state machines.

### Public and private boundary
WDM and KMDF DDIs are documented. Internal WDF object layouts and function tables are not business ABIs and may only be reported with source and version.

### Read-only observation path
Compare WDF bindings, device objects, dispatch tables, and IOCTL capability in Kernel WDF/HAL, I/O Management, and Driver Status.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Each Evt callback has an execution level and synchronization scope. The framework does not turn every callback into PASSIVE_LEVEL or validate every buffer semantic.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: let the framework own object lifetime while defining exactly when each request completes. Incorrect: retain a completed WDFREQUEST, complete twice, or issue KswordARK controls directly from UI code.

### Ksword field interpretation
`frameworkVersion`, `bindingAddress`, `queueState`, and `requestStatus` describe binding, queue, and request state separately; they cannot be collapsed into a single WDF-health verdict.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A WDF binding inside a legitimate module does not validate callback logic, and one successful request says nothing about cancellation, PnP removal, or concurrency paths.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.ioctl_chain.title: The complete IOCTL path and buffering methods
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.ioctl_chain.summa: Follow CTL_CODE and access bits through DeviceIoControl, WDF request creation, length checks, the handler, and completion.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.ioctl_chain.body:
### Object relationship

```text
CTL_CODE -> DeviceIoControl -> IRP_MJ_DEVICE_CONTROL -> dispatch registry -> feature handler -> output
```

### Lifecycle
The caller supplies input and output buffers, the I/O manager establishes METHOD_* transfer state, dispatch locates a handler, and the handler validates version and lengths before completing exactly once.

### Public and private boundary
CTL_CODE layout and the four buffer methods are public. Ksword protocol lives only in `shared/driver`, business handlers register through the registry, and UI code does not duplicate private structures.

### Read-only observation path
Decode device type, function, method, and access in Kernel I/O Management's IOCTL decoder, then verify protocol version and capability in Driver Status.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
METHOD_NEITHER user pointers are untrusted, and a DIRECT I/O MDL only describes locked pages. Handlers still obey request-context and API IRQL limits.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: validate header, version, input length, output capacity, and arithmetic overflow before dispatch. Incorrect: blindly copy a structure, return uninitialized tail bytes, or complete twice.

### Ksword field interpretation
`deviceType/function/method/access` are encoded fields; `protocolVersion`, `bytesReturned`, `lastStatus`, and `unsupported` describe the actual negotiation.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A syntactically valid CTL_CODE does not prove device support, caller rights, buffer safety, or handler success.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.debugging_dumps.t: Kernel debugging, symbols, and crash dumps
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.debugging_dumps.s: Build a safe learning path across KD, WinDbg, PDBs, breakpoints, BugCheck, and dump types.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.debugging_dumps.b:
### Object relationship

```text
Fault/breakpoint -> KD transport or BugCheck -> dump write -> WinDbg + exact PDB -> stacks/objects
```

### Lifecycle
A session configures symbols and transport first. On a crash, the system freezes execution and saves memory according to dump policy; offline analysis then loads symbols matching each module identity.

### Public and private boundary
BugCheck parameters, public structures, and symbol identity are documented. Private fields require a matching PDB GUID/Age or DynData and cannot reuse offsets across builds.

### Read-only observation path
Use Ksword Minidump to inspect headers, modules, BugCheck, and symbol state. The driver BGP path only renders a prepublished snapshot and does not scan live state inside the crash callback.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Kernel debugging changes security posture and timing; complete dumps can contain secrets. BugCheck callbacks run under extreme IRQL and lock constraints and may use only preallocated nonpaged state.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: reproduce on an isolated test machine, preserve exact build and symbol identity, and analyze read-only first. Incorrect: casually break a production host or trust fields decoded with mismatched symbols.

### Ksword field interpretation
`dumpType` controls coverage, `moduleIdentity` and `pdbGuidAge` control symbol confidence, and `missingMemory/partial` mark evidence unavailable from the dump.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A dump is a limited view of one frozen instant. A missing object may have existed earlier, and a clean-looking stack does not make its top module the root cause.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_manager.su: Put object types, headers, directories, names, handle tables, pointer references, and bodies in one relationship map.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_manager.bo:
### Object relationship

```text
Object directory -> named object -> OBJECT_HEADER -> type object + body <- handle table/pointer references
```

### Lifecycle
A create routine allocates and initializes a typed object; insertion makes it openable by name. Handle and pointer references are released separately and the final reference frees it; a temporary object's name can disappear when its last handle closes.

### Public and private boundary
Object, handle, directory, and reference APIs have WDK contracts. `OBJECT_HEADER`, optional headers, and type-index encoding are private and build-specific.

### Read-only observation path
Confirm path and type in Kernel Object Namespace, then compare R3 type statistics with R0 addresses and validation state in Object Type Matrix.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Directory queries depend on access and session context; an object can exit between enumeration and detail lookup. Name queries, allocation, and waits usually require low IRQL.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: hold objects through public reference rules and treat private headers as optional versioned evidence. Incorrect: subtract a fixed constant from every body or retain a raw pointer across asynchronous work.

### Ksword field interpretation
`path/typeName/objectAddress/source/status/typeValidated` separately describe naming, type, transient address, and validation; `objectAddress` is not a persistent identity.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Visibility does not prove a user handle exists, the object can still be opened, its module is malicious, or it survived the race. Absence can reflect access or timing.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_directorie: Explain the roles of the root, Device, Driver, FileSystem, KnownDlls, RPC Control, BaseNamedObjects, and session directories.

### Object relationship

```text
Object root -> Device/Driver/FileSystem/KnownDlls -> Sessions/<n>/BaseNamedObjects or RPC Control
```

### Lifecycle
Boot creates the root and core directories; session creation builds session subtrees, and services/apps insert named objects as needed. Entries can vanish when objects or sessions end.

### Public and private boundary
Object-directory and naming semantics are documented, but the exact directory set and entry layout are not stable ABIs. An object directory is not a disk folder.

### Read-only observation path
Expand Object Namespace, then correlate Directory Recursion, BaseNamedObjects, and Communication Endpoints for path, scope, and query source.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Global, session, and AppContainer scopes differ; a low-rights process may not list or open entries. Enumeration is transient and normally requires a waitable context.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: preserve full object path, session, type, and sample time. Incorrect: merge equal names from separate sessions or treat BaseNamedObjects as a file-system directory.

### Ksword field interpretation
`pathScope/sessionId/type/status/symbolicTarget` describe scope and resolution. Placeholder and budget-truncated nodes differ from an actually empty directory.

### What the evidence cannot prove
No name does not mean no object ever existed or that unnamed objects are absent; a name also does not prove any process retains a handle.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.symbolic_links.ti: Object symbolic links, drive letters, and path conversion
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.symbolic_links.su: Separate Object Manager links, DosDevices/drive letters, volume GUIDs, Win32 paths, and file-system reparse points.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.symbolic_links.bo:
### Object relationship

```text
Win32 path -> DOS-device mapping/object symbolic link -> Device/Volume object -> file-system path
File reparse point ----------------------------------------------^ (different mechanism)
```

### Lifecycle
The system, MountMgr, a driver, or an app creates an object link and removes it on unbind/unload; drive letters can be remapped. A reparse point is persistent file-system metadata.

### Public and private boundary
Object-link query APIs and Win32/NT path rules are documented. Device naming can be driver-defined, so target type cannot be inferred from text alone.

### Read-only observation path
Read full path, target, and query status in Kernel Symbolic Links. Correlate volumes/letters in Storage and inspect a reparse point in File Properties.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Global and local DOS namespaces depend on session and caller context. Path resolution can invoke file-system I/O and belongs at low IRQL.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: resolve layer by layer with cycle/depth budgets. Incorrect: treat an object link as a shortcut or reparse point, or follow a cyclic link without bounds.

### Ksword field interpretation
`objectPath/targetPath/scope/queryStatus/depthLimited` describe object-link resolution; the File page's `reparseTag` comes from a different evidence source.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A target string does not prove the target can be opened, resolves to the same volume, or will not be remapped later.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_header.tit: Versioned parsing of OBJECT_HEADER and optional headers
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_header.sum: Explain why PointerCount, HandleCount, TypeIndex, and optional name/creator/security headers require matching PDB or DynData evidence.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_header.bod:
### Object relationship

```text
Optional headers (Name/Creator/Handle/Security) -> OBJECT_HEADER -> object body
                                                   -> OBJECT_TYPE
```

### Lifecycle
Creation allocates optional headers indicated by flags. Name, security, and counts change over time, and deletion can remove the name before the last reference is released.

### Public and private boundary
Reference and handle semantics are public. Physical header layout, InfoMask, TypeIndex decoding, and security-descriptor storage are private implementations.

### Read-only observation path
In Object Type Matrix and deep object details, read only fields enabled in `fieldFlags`, and inspect DynData profile identity plus per-field status.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
The profile must match the current kernel image. Untrusted addresses use bounded safe copies at no more than APC_LEVEL. Counts change concurrently and are not an atomic multi-field snapshot.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: validate type, address range, and every offset before publishing a complete result. Incorrect: fall back to direct dereference at an old offset or silently normalize absurd counts.

### Ksword field interpretation
`fieldFlags/profileId/typeValidated/pointerCount/handleCount/lastStatus` jointly determine confidence; zero without a validity bit means unknown.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Plausible header fields do not validate the body, and one count mismatch alone does not prove hiding, leakage, or tampering.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_security.t: Security descriptors and object access checks
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_security.s: Build the conceptual flow from tokens, SIDs, DACL/SACL, GenericMapping, and privileges to SeAccessCheck.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.object_security.b:
### Object relationship

```text
Caller token + object security descriptor + desired access/GenericMapping + privileges -> decision + audit
```

### Lifecycle
Creation inherits or sets a security descriptor. Opening performs an access check and stores granted rights in the handle; later token changes do not recalculate an existing handle.

### Public and private boundary
SIDs, ACLs, descriptors, and access-check APIs are documented. Type-specific mappings and some protection policy must be read for the current type/build.

### Read-only observation path
Confirm effective token, integrity, and privileges in Privileges; read `grantedAccess` in Handles; inspect descriptor source and parse state in object details.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
SACL queries require privilege. Impersonation, AppContainer, PPL, and requester mode change outcomes, and complex checks need a waitable context.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: map generic rights for the actual type and validate with the real requester mode. Incorrect: check only Administrators, confuse absent and empty DACLs, or let a driver bypass checks unconditionally.

### Ksword field interpretation
`desiredAccess/grantedAccess/integrityLevel/tokenType/securityStatus` represent different stages; `accessDenied` is the decision, not a cause classification.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A permissive DACL is not proof of exploitation, and denial alone does not identify PPL, policy, or ownership as the protecting mechanism.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.psp_cid_table.sum: Restore PspCidTable to its role as the kernel handle-table root mapping CID space to process/thread objects, not a process list.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.psp_cid_table.bod:
### Object relationship

```text
PID/TID value -> PspCidTable HANDLE_TABLE entry -> EPROCESS or ETHREAD (type validation and reference required)
```

### Lifecycle
Process/thread creation assigns a CID and inserts an entry. Exit removes the mapping, while other references can keep the object alive and the numeric value can later be reused.

### Public and private boundary
CLIENT_ID and supported PID/TID lookup routines are public. The `PspCidTable` symbol, entry layout, and decoding are versioned private evidence.

### Read-only observation path
In Kernel CID Table, inspect R3 snapshot, active list, CID rows, type validation, reference status, creation time, and traversal budget together.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Walk only with matching DynData capability, safe reads at no more than APC_LEVEL, and creation-time handling for exit races and ID reuse.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: decode read-only and then revalidate through a supported object-reference path. Incorrect: equate CID visibility with an active process or modify/clear an entry to handle hiding.

### Ksword field interpretation
`cid/entryKind/objectAddress/typeValidated/referenceStatus/creationTime/truncated` form one CID evidence row; missing components lower confidence.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A CID row does not prove the object still runs, is visible to user mode, is hidden, or is malicious. A missing row can be a normal exit race.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.cid_object_relati: PID, TID, HANDLE, CLIENT_ID, and objects
Explain when an integer is an ID, handle, or index and when an EPROCESS/ETHREAD reference is required.

### Object relationship

```text
CLIENT_ID = {UniqueProcess, UniqueThread}
PID -> EPROCESS; TID -> ETHREAD -> owning EPROCESS; HANDLE -> object in one process's table
```

### Lifecycle
PID/TID values are unique only during an object's active interval and can be reused. A handle matters only in its owner process and open interval; an object reference can extend lifetime.

### Public and private boundary
CLIENT_ID and lookup/reference routines have public semantics. CID encoding and internal object fields are not stable interfaces.

### Read-only observation path
In CID Table, separate process/thread by `kind`, correlate a thread's `parentPid`, object address, and creation time, then confirm the same identity in process details.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Joining snapshots by number alone is vulnerable to reuse. After referencing an object, query fields only at supported IRQL and release it on every path.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: build identity from type, ID, and creation time and validate ownership. Incorrect: open a process with a TID or interpret a user handle as a CID index.

### Ksword field interpretation
`kind/cid/tid/parentPid/objectAddress/processObjectAddress/creationTime` assign roles to each number; equal displayed values do not imply equal semantics.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Equal numeric values do not identify one object. A matching thread owner also does not prove the thread is running or its start address is trustworthy.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.handle_table_tabl: Explain how an encoded root, levels, and paged entries locate objects while preserving strict read-only validation.

### Object relationship

```text
HANDLE_TABLE.TableCode -> level 0/1/2 root pages -> HANDLE_TABLE_ENTRY -> encoded object pointer/attributes
```

### Lifecycle
The table grows levels and pages on demand; allocation and close update entries and free slots can be reused while a traversal is in progress.

### Public and private boundary
Handle semantics are public. TableCode low-bit levels, entry bitfields, and pointer encoding are private version implementations described by a matching profile.

### Read-only observation path
In CID or deep Handles, check `capability/profile` first, then visited/returned/limit, per-entry decode status, type validation, and reference result.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Walk only at safe-read IRQL with page and entry budgets. Every failed read marks partial; there is no raw-dereference fallback.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: validate alignment, range, arithmetic overflow, and repeated pages at each level. Incorrect: trust bit patterns, walk a damaged tree without bounds, or teach pointer-bit modification.

### Ksword field interpretation
`tableCode/level/handleIndex/entryFlags/lookupStatus/referenceStatus/visitedBudget` expose the traversal and validation, not merely an address.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Finishing the current levels does not create an atomic snapshot. An odd entry can be close-race, profile mismatch, or read failure rather than tampering.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.process_cross_vie: Compare public snapshots, PsActiveProcessHead, PspCidTable, and thread ownership while explaining differences.

### Object relationship

```text
Public process/thread snapshot <-> active process list <-> PspCidTable <-> ETHREAD owner
```

### Lifecycle
Each source samples at a different instant. Creation and exit create short windows visible in only some sources, and ID reuse can make an old number identify a new object.

### Public and private boundary
Public snapshots and supported references are stable. Active-list, CID-root, and private creation-time fields depend on DynData, and every source can be partial.

### Read-only observation path
Refresh CID Table, read source flags and snapshot time first, then validate PID/TID, type, creation time, object address, and difference class per row.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
A protected process can block R3 details without being hidden. R0 traversal is offset-, budget-, and race-limited, so sources must belong to the same sample generation.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: label a source-only row as unexplained and resample. Incorrect: call every difference a rootkit or treat asynchronous snapshots as one transaction.

### Ksword field interpretation
`sourceMask/differenceClass/typeValidated/creationTime/snapshotId/partial/truncated` determine evidence strength; names are supporting text only.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A one-time cross-view difference is not proof of hiding or tampering, and agreement cannot exclude every short-lived object, filter, or uncovered source.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.process_vs_cid_ha: Per-process handle tables versus the global CID table
Separate each process's ObjectTable resource handles from PspCidTable's system process/thread ID mapping.

### Object relationship

```text
EPROCESS.ObjectTable -> that process's file/event/process HANDLEs
PspCidTable ---------> system CID values to EPROCESS/ETHREAD
```

### Lifecycle
Process handles can be created, inherited, duplicated, and closed and are cleaned at process exit. CID entries follow process/thread object lifetime and are not caller-opened resource handles.

### Public and private boundary
DuplicateHandle, inheritance, and access masks are public. Both HANDLE_TABLE roots and entry decoders are private and derive meaning from their source.

### Read-only observation path
Handles enumerates one process's ObjectTable; CID enumerates system identities. Use page title, source, and entry kind to avoid mixing the records.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Per-process enumeration is access- and exit-race-limited; CID traversal is DynData-limited. The kernel-handle flag can also select a different owner table.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: establish whose table, what key, and what target type first. Incorrect: apply one ExHandleTable interpretation to both roots or treat closing a process handle as deleting a PID.

### Ksword field interpretation
Per-process `ownerPid/handleValue/grantedAccess` and CID `cid/entryKind/referenceStatus` are separate field groups and should not be merged.

### What the evidence cannot prove
No handle from a process does not prove no interaction, and a CID entry does not prove any user process holds a handle to that object.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.cross_view_visual: Require source, type validation, reference, creation time, difference class, budget, and DynData to remain visible together.

### Object relationship

```text
Multi-source raw rows -> identity normalization -> validation/budget flags -> difference class -> human review
```

### Lifecycle
Each refresh creates a separate snapshotId; old rows become stale when capture starts and a complete batch is published together. Sorting/filtering must not change source identity.

### Public and private boundary
UI may normalize public and private sources but cannot invent missing fields. DynData version, query status, and source must survive into the final row.

### Read-only observation path
Read sample time, budget, and partial state in CID summary before source and difference columns; clear filters and repeat a sample when necessary.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Large tables need traversal and display budgets; asynchronous fill applies only to the matching generation. Unsupported/access-denied and truly empty require distinct states.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: use neutral classes such as R0-only, R3-only, and review required. Incorrect: replace validation with a red malicious badge or hide truncation/read failures.

### Ksword field interpretation
`sourceMask/typeValidated/referenceStatus/creationTime/differenceClass/visited/returned/truncated/profileId` is the minimum complete field group.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Visualization improves readability but not source strength; color, sort order, and rule matches are not maliciousness verdicts.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.executive_thread_: Separate executive objects from scheduler subobjects and assign ownership of address space, token, object table, active list, and thread list.

### Object relationship

```text
EPROCESS (executive process) contains KPROCESS (scheduler) and owns address space/token/ObjectTable
ETHREAD (executive thread) contains KTHREAD (scheduler) and references its EPROCESS
```

### Lifecycle
Process creation establishes the executive object and address space before the first thread. A thread can stop scheduling before its object dies, and handles/references can retain it; process release follows thread and resource cleanup.

### Public and private boundary
PEPROCESS/PETHREAD are public opaque pointer types. Field layout, embedded KPROCESS/KTHREAD offsets, and lists are private DynData.

### Read-only observation path
Read PID, creation time, token, and thread list in process details, then correlate process/thread addresses, type validation, and ownership in CID Table.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Query fields only while holding a reference; some queries require PASSIVE_LEVEL. Offsets differ between builds and an exiting object can remain delete-pending.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: obtain references through supported lookup and treat private fields as optional enrichment. Incorrect: use EPROCESS address as permanent identity or walk an unlocked thread list without bounds.

### Ksword field interpretation
`processObject/threadObject/parentPid/creationTime/typeValidated/referenceStatus` describe relationships; CPU and memory statistics are a different sample.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Existence does not mean schedulable, active-list presence does not make every field coherent, and a missing private field is not proof of hiding.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.process_lifecycle: Follow CreateProcess through image mapping, first thread, notifications, exit, and final object release to distinguish events from snapshots.

### Object relationship

```text
CreateProcess -> process/address space -> image map -> create notification -> first thread -> run -> exit notification -> final reference
```

### Lifecycle
Many checks and notifications occur before the API returns. Exit terminates threads, tears down address space, and notifies listeners, while handles, jobs, or kernel references can delay object release.

### Public and private boundary
Process, thread, and image notification APIs and callback constraints are public. Exact internal stages and private-field order are not cross-version contracts.

### Read-only observation path
Compare the current process snapshot with event history using PID plus creation time, then revalidate object state in CID Table; a notification log is not a current enumeration.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Callbacks run in defined process/thread contexts and must not block for long. A short-lived process may appear only in events; process protection can restrict details without changing the lifecycle.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: events record identity and time while snapshots answer what exists now. Incorrect: call one missed callback hiding or merge a reused PID into an old record.

### Ksword field interpretation
`eventTime/snapshotTime/creationTime/exitTime/sourceMask` distinguish events and state; `isExited` does not mean object storage is already freed.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Create/exit notifications do not capture every action in between, and absence from a current sample does not mean the process never ran.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.scheduler.title: Scheduling, priority, and CPU affinity
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.scheduler.summary: Separate priority, quantum, ready state, processor groups, affinity, ideal processor, context switches, and sampled statistics.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.scheduler.body:
### Object relationship

```text
Thread priority/affinity/state -> per-CPU scheduling decision -> running/ready/waiting -> context switch -> time statistics
```

### Lifecycle
A thread moves among ready, running, and waiting. Dynamic priority and quantum change; group and affinity limit candidate CPUs but do not promise the next execution CPU.

### Public and private boundary
Priority and affinity APIs are public. Per-CPU ready queues, scheduler locks, and private KTHREAD fields are not stable ABIs.

### Read-only observation path
Read priority, group, and affinity in process/thread details, inspect system-thread candidates and module entry in Work-Queue Threads, and compare CPU time across several samples.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Systems above 64 logical processors require processor-group semantics. Rights and process protection limit queries, and scheduler fields are only instantaneous under concurrency.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: interpret CPU percentage as a time-window statistic. Incorrect: infer fixed binding from current/ideal processor or label a high-priority thread abnormal by itself.

### Ksword field interpretation
`basePriority/dynamicPriority/group/affinity/idealProcessor/cpuDelta/sampleInterval` describe constraints and statistics, not a future scheduling decision.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Low CPU does not mean no execution, high priority does not mean malicious, and an affinity mask does not prove the thread ran on every allowed CPU.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.dispatcher_object: Dispatcher objects and the wait model
Explain signaled state for events, mutexes, semaphores, timers, threads, wait blocks, and KeWaitFor*.

### Object relationship

```text
Thread KWAIT_BLOCK -> dispatcher object (Event/Mutex/Semaphore/Timer/Thread) -> signaled state -> wakeup
```

### Lifecycle
An object starts in a defined signal state. A thread registers wait blocks and waits; setting/releasing the object makes candidates ready. No waiter or user may remain when the object is destroyed.

### Public and private boundary
KEVENT, KMUTEX, KSEMAPHORE, KTIMER, and wait APIs have public contracts. Dispatcher-header and wait-queue internals are not fixed-offset mutation targets.

### Read-only observation path
Inspect KTIMER/KDPC links in Timer/DPC and wait reasons in thread details; a named event may also be correlated in Object Namespace.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Code at DISPATCH_LEVEL or higher cannot wait for a dispatcher object. Alertable waits, APCs, and timeouts change the return path.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: loop on the business predicate and handle timeout/cancellation. Incorrect: treat wakeup as a persistent resource, wait under an incompatible lock, or destroy an object with waiters.

### Ksword field interpretation
`objectType/signalState/waitReason/dueTime/period/routineAddress` come from different layers; do not invent waiter counts when no queue field exists.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Currently signaled does not guarantee which thread runs first, and no observed waiter does not exclude past blocking or a wait beginning immediately after capture.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.apc_dpc_work_item: Execution timing of APCs, DPCs, and work items
Separate user/kernel/special APCs, DPCs, and worker threads rather than treating them as interchangeable asynchronous calls.

### Object relationship

```text
APC -> selected thread context (subject to user/kernel APC conditions)
DPC -> selected CPU at DISPATCH_LEVEL
Work item -> system worker thread at PASSIVE_LEVEL
```

### Lifecycle
Initialize and queue the object, run when dispatch conditions hold, and cancel only before execution ownership transfers. Unload must cancel or drain every callback.

### Public and private boundary
Contracts such as KeInsertQueueDpc and IoQueueWorkItem are public. Private system queues and KAPC/KDPC/KTHREAD fields are bounded read-only evidence.

### Read-only observation path
Correlate DPC routine and module in Timer/DPC and thread entry/candidate reason in Work-Queue Threads; a user APC additionally depends on target-thread state.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
A DPC cannot wait or touch pageable memory; a work item may wait but consumes a shared worker. A user APC usually needs an alertable wait.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: high IRQL queues minimal work while retaining context references. Incorrect: pass a stack pointer to delayed work, block in DPC, or equate successful APC queueing with execution.

### Ksword field interpretation
`queueType/processor/routineAddress/module/threadId/state/cancelled` describe queue and observation; state values from different mechanisms are not directly comparable.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A registered/queued item may not have run, and an absent one may have completed or executed in a private path between samples.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.process_attach.su: Explain KAPC_STATE, object references, exception cleanup, and complex operations prohibited while attached.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.process_attach.bo:
### Object relationship

```text
Current thread + referenced target EPROCESS -> KeStackAttachProcess/KAPC_STATE -> temporary target address space -> KeUnstackDetachProcess
```

### Lifecycle
Reference the target and prepare state, attach briefly for the minimum memory operation, then detach in stack order and release on success, exception, and cancellation.

### Public and private boundary
KeStackAttachProcess is documented and explicitly cautioned. Address-space internals and APC-state layout are not fields to write manually.

### Read-only observation path
Lock target identity with PID plus creation time in process details; memory reads report actual byte count and error, with R0 identity-revalidation state beside them.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Run below DISPATCH_LEVEL and keep the attached region tiny. Complex waits, asynchronous I/O, and APC-blocking operations can deadlock; exiting targets need identity checks.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: use RAII or one cleanup exit to guarantee detach. Incorrect: issue complex I/O while attached, miss exception cleanup, or break nested detach order.

### Ksword field interpretation
`targetPid/expectedCreateTime/identityStatus/bytesRequested/bytesRead/lastStatus` describe target and copy; a success flag never replaces the length.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A successful read does not make the page stable, trusted, or wholly readable, and attachment grants no right to bypass isolation.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.session_silo_pico: Show how interactive sessions, job/container Silos, AppContainer capabilities, and Pico providers alter the ordinary process view.

### Object relationship

```text
System -> Session -> WindowStation/Desktop
       -> Server Silo/Job -> container processes
Token -> AppContainer SID/capabilities; Pico process -> provider such as WSL
```

### Lifecycle
A session, job, or Silo establishes namespace/resource boundaries before processes join. Cleanup can lag the final member. A Pico provider manages a specialized system-call model.

### Public and private boundary
Session IDs, jobs, AppContainer tokens, and selected container APIs are public. Silo/Pico objects and private fields need versioned evidence.

### Read-only observation path
Read session, job, token/AppContainer, and image kind in process details, then correlate Sessions/BaseNamedObjects scope in Object Namespace.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Cross-session/container queries face access and namespace limits; WSL implementation changes. Missing private fields remain unsupported rather than guessed.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: display session, silo, and container as separate dimensions. Incorrect: call every nonzero SessionId a container, equate AppContainer with low integrity, or call Pico hidden.

### Ksword field interpretation
`sessionId/jobId/appContainerSid/capabilities/siloId/processKind/source` describe distinct isolation layers; empty values need query status.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Container or Pico membership is not suspicious by itself, and an R3 namespace omission can be isolation rather than hiding.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.page_tables.title: Page tables, large pages, and LA57
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.page_tables.summa: Explain translation from CR3 and PML4/PML5 through PTE/PFN, NX/RW/US/Global, and 2-MB/1-GB pages.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.page_tables.body:
### Object relationship

```text
Virtual address + CR3 -> optional PML5 -> PML4 -> PDPT -> PD -> PT -> PFN + page offset
                               1-GB page ends at PDPTE; 2-MB page ends at PDE
```

### Lifecycle
Address-space creation establishes top-level tables. Mapping, faults, and protection updates change entries and invalidate TLBs; exit frees table pages and PFNs can be reused.

### Public and private boundary
Architectural bits are public. Windows self-map, prototype PTE, and software-state implementation changes, so four levels cannot be hard-coded as universal.

### Read-only observation path
Confirm region/protection in Memory, then read translation level, page size, permissions, and source in SLAT/IOMMU; report the failing level rather than only zero.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Use the correct process CR3 and coherent CPU/address space. LA57, KVA shadow, Hyper-V, and large pages alter the path; page-table reads must avoid invalid physical access.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: check canonical address, present/large bits, boundaries, and overflow at every level. Incorrect: always walk four levels, call transition/prototype hardware-present, or teach PTE writing.

### Ksword field interpretation
`level/pageSize/present/readWrite/user/nx/global/pfn/translationStatus` belongs in a per-level view; physical address is valid only on success.

### What the evidence cannot prove
An executable PTE is not proof of execution or malice, and a successful translation can change with the mapping or TLB immediately afterward.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.page_fault_workin: Page faults, working sets, and memory lists
Separate soft/hard faults, working sets, standby/modified/zeroed/free lists, compression, and trimming to avoid occupancy mistakes.

### Object relationship

```text
Virtual access -> PTE state -> soft fault (resident/mapped) or hard fault (storage read)
Process working set <-> standby/modified/free/zeroed/compression store
```

### Lifecycle
Commit is not immediate residency. Access faults pages into a working set; trimming moves them to standby/modified, writeback permits reuse, and compressed pages still consume system memory.

### Public and private boundary
Performance counters and working-set query APIs are public. Internal lists, compression store, and software PTE states are version implementations.

### Read-only observation path
Compare working set, private bytes, and fault deltas over a window in process performance, then inspect system physical-list totals in Memory.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Counters are samples affected by access, compression policy, NUMA, and load. Fault handling can wait and must not be induced casually at high IRQL.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: report commit, resident, private, shared, and fault rate separately. Incorrect: call working set exclusive physical use or every page fault disk I/O.

### Ksword field interpretation
`workingSet/privateBytes/commit/pageFaultDelta/hardFaultDelta/sampleInterval` must share a window; cumulative totals are not instantaneous rates.

### What the evidence cannot prove
High working set is not proof of a leak, high fault count is not proof of disk failure, and one statistic cannot identify a VAD/page source.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.vad.title: VAD trees and virtual-region semantics
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.vad.summary: Explain Virtual Address Descriptors, MEM_PRIVATE/IMAGE/MAPPED, protections, reserve/commit, and VirtualQuery evidence limits.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.vad.body:
### Object relationship

```text
Process address space -> VAD interval tree -> private / image section / mapped section -> PTE/working-set pages
```

### Lifecycle
VirtualAlloc or section mapping creates/splits VADs; protection and commit change ranges. Unmap removes nodes, while references and concurrent queries create transient differences.

### Public and private boundary
VirtualQuery region/type/protection is public. Kernel VAD nodes, tree implementation, and private flags are read-only data under matching DynData.

### Read-only observation path
Inspect VirtualQuery by address in Memory, then correlate executable/private ranges with modules, mapped files, page tables, and thread start addresses.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Cross-process access and exit must be handled. Kernel traversal needs proper synchronization or a safe snapshot and cannot induce paging at high IRQL.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: validate ordered, nonoverlapping, nonoverflowing ranges and retain source. Incorrect: call every `MEM_PRIVATE + EXECUTE` malicious or write old VAD fields.

### Ksword field interpretation
`base/end/regionSize/type/protection/commit/mappedPath/source/partial` describes a range; missing path does not automatically mean anonymous.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A VAD states range policy, not that every page is resident, content-consistent, executed, or unchanged during the query.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.pfn_database.titl: The PFN database and physical-page evidence
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.pfn_database.summ: Explain page-frame numbers, reference/share counts, page location, and reverse-mapping value and version risk.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.pfn_database.body:
### Object relationship

```text
PTE/MDL -> PFN -> PFN database entry -> page location/ref/share/owner hints -> physical page
```

### Lifecycle
A page moves among zeroed/free/standby/modified/active states. Mapping, I/O, and locking change counts; after reuse the same PFN can contain unrelated data.

### Public and private boundary
PFN numbers and MDL page arrays have public uses. PFN database address, entry bitfields, and reverse mapping are highly version-specific internals.

### Read-only observation path
Derive a PFN from a validated virtual address/page table or MDL, then inspect source, valid fields, budget, and profile in SLAT/IOMMU rather than blindly scanning the database.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Read only matching fields under strict page budgets; counts change concurrently and safe-read failure marks partial. Physical access is also bounded by VBS/IOMMU and device ranges.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: perform bounded correlation from a trusted root. Incorrect: treat an entry as stable ownership, infer purpose from a name, or modify count/location bits.

### Ksword field interpretation
`pfn/pageLocation/referenceCount/shareCount/fieldFlags/profileId/readStatus` jointly determine what is interpretable; unknown bits stay unknown.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A process mapping does not make a PFN private or malicious; unusual counts can reflect sampling, profile mismatch, or legitimate locking.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.section_control_a: Connect file/image mappings, Subsections, prototype PTEs, copy-on-write, deleted images, cache, and reclamation.

### Object relationship

```text
Section object -> ControlArea -> Subsection -> prototype PTEs -> process VAD/PTEs
                    <-> FileObject/SectionObjectPointers/cache
```

### Lifecycle
A section connects a file or paging store; a view creates a VAD and copy-on-write creates private pages. Handle, view, and cache references release separately before ControlArea reclamation, and deletion can remain pending.

### Public and private boundary
Section/view and file-mapping APIs are public. ControlArea/Subsection/prototype-PTE layout and counts are private PDB evidence.

### Read-only observation path
Confirm FileObject and process views in file mapping/occupancy, MEM_IMAGE/MAPPED in Memory, and validated ControlArea fields in deep object audit.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Close, unmap, and reclamation race. Private-field queries need a matching profile, low IRQL, and bounded safe reads without waiting under incompatible file-system locks.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: track section handles, mapped views, file references, and cache state separately. Incorrect: equate handle close with image unload or diagnose a leak from one count.

### Ksword field interpretation
`sectionType/viewCount/sectionRef/fileObject/controlArea/fieldFlags/deletePending` come from distinct layers; zero requires validity state.

### What the evidence cannot prove
A mapped deleted image is not automatically malicious. A ControlArea does not prove file content stability, identical views, or residency.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.mdl_dma.title: MDLs, DMA, and the IOMMU
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.mdl_dma.summary: Show that an MDL describes a buffer's physical-page layout and connect locking, system mappings, scatter/gather, DMA adapters, and IOMMU.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.mdl_dma.body:
### Object relationship

```text
Virtual buffer -> MDL/PFN array -> locked pages/system map -> scatter-gather -> DMA adapter -> IOMMU -> device
```

### Lifecycle
Allocate an MDL, build or probe/lock it according to origin, optionally map it and create a DMA mapping, then unmap DMA, system mapping, pages, and descriptor in reverse order.

### Public and private boundary
MDL, DMA adapter, and scatter/gather DDIs are documented; most MDL fields are semi-opaque. Private IOMMU tables/domains are not guessed mutation targets.

### Read-only observation path
Start with a concrete I/O or executable-memory record's MDL source, then correlate device, DMAR/IVRS capability, and runtime state in SLAT/IOMMU.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Probe user pages in requester context under exception handling; mapping and DMA APIs each have IRQL contracts. Firmware, Hyper-V, and policy can jointly manage the IOMMU.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: treat the MDL as a descriptor and own lock/map transitions. Incorrect: treat its address as data, unlock twice, free during DMA, or equate CPU physical and device bus address.

### Ksword field interpretation
`byteCount/byteOffset/pfnCount/locked/mapped/dmaDomain/iommuStatus/source` describe stages; without a device mapping, do not claim DMA reachability.

### What the evidence cannot prove
An MDL does not prove DMA occurred, content is malicious, or IOMMU protection is absent; enabled IOMMU also does not validate every mapping policy.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.pool.title: Paged/nonpaged pool and pool tags
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.pool.summary: Explain pool types, tags, quota, Special Pool, overruns, and leak evidence without assigning ownership from a tag name alone.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.pool.body:
### Object relationship

```text
Driver/kernel component -> pool allocation(type,size,tag,quota) -> use -> free
                                          -> optional Special Pool/Verifier
```

### Lifecycle
Allocation returns a typed/tagged block and a compatible routine releases it. Caches can retain blocks; a leak is a time-series failure to return memory, not simply one large snapshot.

### Public and private boundary
ExAllocatePool2, tags, and Verifier contracts are public. Pool headers, segmented heap, and accounting internals change and are not fixed-offset write targets.

### Read-only observation path
Inspect address, size, tag, type, module range, and multi-snapshot deltas in Pool/Big Pool and executable-memory views; use Verifier only on a test host when needed.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Paged pool is inaccessible at DISPATCH_LEVEL; nonpaged does not mean executable. Allocation APIs, NX defaults, and implementation evolve by Windows release.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: attribute by stack/module/time trend and verify allocate/free pairing. Incorrect: blame a driver from four tag characters or call every increase a leak.

### Ksword field interpretation
`address/size/tag/poolType/nonExecutable/source/module/firstSeen/snapshotDelta` supports attribution; a tag is caller-supplied.

### What the evidence cannot prove
One large allocation is not proof of leak or malice, legitimate caches grow, and a tag can be shared or forged.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.executable_memory: Evidence strength for executable kernel memory
Grade module sections, RX/RWX private mappings, Big Pool, System PTE, and MDL origins instead of directly declaring malice.

### Object relationship

```text
Executable address -> loaded module section / private system map / Big Pool / System PTE / MDL map
                   -> content, permissions, origin, baseline, and references -> confidence
```

### Lifecycle
Image load and runtime mapping create executable regions; hotpatch/JIT/security software can legitimately change content. Addresses can be reused after unload/unmap, so evidence binds to a snapshot.

### Public and private boundary
PE sections, module ranges, and some protections are public. System-PTE/Big-Pool/MDL attribution requires versioned safe reads; write-protection bypass is outside the teaching path.

### Read-only observation path
Compare relocated clean images in Code Integrity, then correlate pool, page tables, signature, callback/hook targets, and executable-memory origin.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Full scans have budgets and can be partial. Reads avoid invalid/pageable addresses and select baselines by image identity; VBS/HVCI changes permitted mappings.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: grade origin confidence, content difference, and independent correlations. Incorrect: report rootkit from RWX, outside-module, or unknown tag alone, or modify pages automatically.

### Ksword field interpretation
`origin/protection/module/section/cleanHash/observedHash/differenceClass/readStatus/partial` form the evidence; `unknown` means investigate, not malicious.

### What the evidence cannot prove
Executable memory outside a module is not proof of execution or malice, and disk equality does not validate signature, call path, or runtime behavior.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.irp_lifecycle.sum: Connect creation, stack locations, Major/Minor functions, forwarding, pending, cancellation, completion, MDLs, and final completion order.
context_translations.kernel.knowledge.topic.irp_lifecycle.bod:
### Object relationship

```text
I/O manager -> IRP + IO_STACK_LOCATION[n] -> upper/filter/function/bus drivers -> reverse completion -> caller
```

### Lifecycle
The I/O manager or a driver allocates an IRP. Each stack layer reads its parameters and completes, queues, or forwards it. A pending request completes exactly once, completion routines run back up the stack, and cancellation races with completion.

### Public and private boundary
IRPs, stack locations, and standard Major/Minor contracts are public. Driver-private contexts and undocumented flags cannot be guessed across modules. A KMDF request still rests on this lifecycle.

### Read-only observation path
Decode Major/Minor and IOCTL in I/O Management, inspect stack and dispatch tables in Device/Driver Objects, and correlate start, pending, completion, and status in file-monitor records.

### Version, privilege, and IRQL limits
Allowed IRQL differs by dispatch and completion path; cancellation routines, DPCs, and user buffers are particularly constrained. PnP and Power IRPs have specific forwarding/completion rules.

### Correct and incorrect handling
Correct: define IRP ownership, when pending is marked, cancellation synchronization, and final completer. Incorrect: complete twice, omit pending propagation, use the IRP after completion, or return the wrong completion code.

### Ksword field interpretation
`major/minor/stackIndex/pending/cancelled/completionStatus/information/bytesReturned` describe stages; final status cannot reconstruct every intermediate layer.

### What the evidence cannot prove
One completed IRP does not prove every layer was observed, cancellation is race-free, or the device physically completed the operation.
